intro: Leaf beets are a useful answer for gardeners who like spinach but find true spinach quick to bolt or difficult in dry weather. Swiss chard, seakale beet, spinach beet and perpetual spinach are all grown for leaves rather than swollen roots, and a few plants can provide many pickings over a long season. Swiss chard has broad leaves with thick, edible midribs, often white but sometimes red, yellow or pink, and it is ornamental enough for the flower border. Spinach beet has a plainer green leaf, is used much like spinach in the kitchen. The main rule is to pick regularly: small leaves are tender and useful for salads or cooking, while over-large leaves become tougher and the plant slows down.

Broccoli covers several related crops rather than just the green heads sold in supermarkets. Summer and autumn crops are mostly calabrese, which forms a central green head followed by side shoots, while winter and spring crops are usually purple or white sprouting broccoli, grown for a long succession of small spears when other fresh greens are scarce. Garden broccoli may not look as blemish-free as shop-bought heads, and summer crops often need protection from caterpillars and pigeons, but the flavour and the long season make it well worth growing.

Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like buds produced up a tall stem, maturing gradually through autumn and winter. A freshly picked sprout from the garden is a midwinter treat, often sweeter and nuttier than shop-bought sprouts, and small firm buttons can be good raw as well as cooked. Success depends less on complicated technique than on firm, fertile soil, careful transplanting and steady growth.

Cabbage is one of the most versatile brassicas, and with the right choice of variety it can provide food for much of the year. Spring cabbages give tender greens and small heads before many other vegetables are ready; summer and autumn cabbages provide fresh heads for salads, slaws and cooking; winter, savoy and red cabbages can stand or store into the colder months. The key is to match the variety to the season, because cabbage types differ in shape, texture, colour, hardiness and speed of hearting.
